chapters.title: A web page: source, browser and server
chapters.mental:
HTML is a markup language: it names the structure and meaning of a document. CSS is a style language that controls how that structure is presented. JavaScript is a programming language executed by the browser or another host. PHP is a programming language commonly executed by a server. A visitor receives the server's response, not the PHP source that generated it. These layers can cooperate without becoming interchangeable.

A browser parses HTML into a document tree, applies style rules and paints pixels. A server accepts a request and returns a response. Opening a local preview exercises the browser portion; it does not demonstrate a network request, authentication or a server database. Our first document is deliberately small enough to inspect every character and every visible element.
chapters.anatomy:
An element such as `

Hello

` has an opening tag, content and a closing tag. The tag names the kind of content. A document begins with `` to request standards rendering, then an `html` root containing `head` metadata and `body` visible content. The `title` labels the browser document, while an `h1` labels the visible topic. Whitespace in ordinary text is generally collapsed, so source indentation helps humans without creating layout.
examples: Read the tag boundaries before considering appearance.
One text paragraph; the angle-bracket markup is not shown.
Both titles matter, but they occupy different places.
The document title and visible heading can differ.
tasks: Predict which text from the first example is visible.
Only Hello, web. appears as paragraph text.
Change a paragraph without changing the document title.
The visible body changes while the browser document title remains the same.
Build a complete document with a title, one heading and two paragraphs.
The preview contains one main heading and two paragraphs in a main region.
Explain why PHP source pasted into an HTML page does not execute on a PHP server.
A browser preview parses HTML; no PHP interpreter or server request was involved.

Document structure and readable text remain; meaning does not depend on CSS.
Trace a requested page from source to visible output.
Distinguish server response bytes, parsed document tree, applied style and painted output.
chapters.mistakes: Do not call every file a website or every successful preview a deployed server. Inspect the actual title and body separately. Closing a paragraph with the wrong tag may be repaired by the parser, producing a different tree than the source suggests.

chapters.title: Elements, attributes, nesting and text escaping
chapters.mental:
An attribute adds information to an opening tag. In `<html lang="en">`, the attribute name is lang and its value identifies the document language. Attribute values should be quoted consistently. Nesting means one element's content contains another element; the resulting parent-child relationship matters to styling, accessibility and scripts. A paragraph can contain emphasized text, but a list does not belong inside that paragraph.

HTML has special syntax characters. A less-than sign begins markup, so literal comparison text may need `<`. An ampersand begins a character reference and is commonly represented as `&`. Escaping means representing text so a parser treats it as data. It is different from deleting characters and different from making an unsafe URL safe.
chapters.anatomy: Close nested elements in reverse order: open paragraph, open strong, close strong, close paragraph. Void elements such as `br` and `img` have no closing tag. A `data-*` attribute stores page-specific metadata; it does not create a visible label. `id` must uniquely identify an element in the document. Class names may repeat because they group related elements.
examples: The strong element identifies importance within the paragraph.
The word before has semantic importance and typically bold styling.
Character references preserve the intended data.
tasks: Predict the text content after character references are parsed.
The browser displays comparison signs and an ampersand, not the entity source.
Add a language attribute and explain its role.
The root lang attribute identifies the language for pronunciation and processing.
Build a notes paragraph with nested importance and literal angle brackets.
The structure remains a paragraph and the comparison is text rather than an element.
Repair overlapping emphasis tags by drawing their tree.
Each opened element is closed before its parent closes.
Add two related notes without duplicating an id.
Shared class names group them while each id remains unique.
Explain escaping versus validation with a text and URL example.
Escaping preserves literal text; URL validation separately restricts allowed schemes and destinations.
chapters.mistakes: A page that looks correct can still contain an unintended parser repair. Inspect the Elements tree rather than relying only on View Source. Never teach `innerHTML` as a general way to insert untrusted text.

chapters.title: Semantic structure, headings and landmarks
chapters.mental:
Semantic markup tells the browser and reader what a piece of content is. A main region contains the page's primary content. Navigation groups major navigation links; a header introduces a page or section; a footer provides related closing information. These elements are not a promise of any particular position on screen. A header can appear inside an article and need not be a fixed top bar.

Headings provide a hierarchy that a screen reader and a visual reader can use to scan. Use the main topic as h1 and its major subdivisions as h2, with h3 for nested detail. Choose levels for structure, not because the browser's default font size looks attractive. A section normally benefits from a heading; a generic div is appropriate when there is no additional semantic meaning.
chapters.anatomy: Draw the content outline before assigning tags. Use one visible main region for the primary task. Give repeated navigation regions distinct accessible labels such as `aria-label="Course"`. A skip link points to the main region's id and lets a keyboard user bypass repeated controls. Native HTML supplies roles automatically; redundant roles rarely add value.
examples: HTML is a subsection of Study notes.
The fragment targets a real unique element.
The link moves to the main content target without a network request.
tasks: Draw the heading outline of the first example.
Study notes contains HTML as one second-level section.
Add a sibling CSS section at the correct level.
CSS and HTML both use h2 because they have the same parent topic.
Build a study page with landmarks and a working skip link.
Header, labeled navigation, one main and footer have meaningful content; the skip target exists.
Replace a heading used only for large text with an appropriate element.
A visual callout uses CSS without corrupting the document outline.
Check the document with CSS disabled or unavailable.
The reading order and heading relationships remain coherent.
Explain when a div is more appropriate than section.
Use a generic container when grouping does not introduce a meaningful headed section.
chapters.mistakes: A semantic element cannot compensate for misleading content. Avoid h1-h4 jumps that merely chase font sizes. Do not create dozens of named landmarks for tiny fragments because navigation becomes noisy.

chapters.title: Links, paths, navigation and usable destinations
chapters.mental:
A URL identifies a resource and can contain a scheme, host, path, query and fragment. A relative path is resolved against a base URL; it is not resolved against the author's mental picture of a folder. A fragment such as #methods identifies a location within the current document and does not require another document to exist. An anchor with href provides navigation semantics and keyboard behavior automatically.

Good link text tells a reader the destination or action. A page full of links named click here loses meaning when links are read as a list. A link navigates; a button changes application state or submits an action. Styling a paragraph blue does not create link behavior, and adding a click listener does not automatically provide keyboard support.
chapters.anatomy: Use `href="#details"` with a unique `id="details"` for this offline lesson. A leading slash means a path from the origin root, while `../` moves one directory upward relative to the base path. Production external links may need a new-window notice and suitable rel values; do not open new tabs by default merely to keep a user on your site.
examples: A fragment is enough for a self-contained document.
The navigation target is the methods section.
Choose the element before its styling.
The link navigates; the button requires an implemented action.
tasks: Resolve ../images/plot.svg from /notes/week1/page.html.
The resolved path is /notes/images/plot.svg on the same origin.
Replace vague link text with destination-specific wording.
The link makes sense outside its surrounding sentence.
Build a contents list that navigates to three local sections.
Every fragment matches one unique section id and works with keyboard activation.
Diagnose a link whose fragment has no matching id.
The link has no intended target even if its visual style looks correct.
Distinguish a disabled action from an unavailable destination.
A button can be disabled; a meaningful alternative explanation should replace a dead link.
Explain the difference between absolute, root-relative and document-relative paths.
Each has a distinct base and can resolve differently when the document moves.
chapters.mistakes: Do not test relative paths only from an editor preview with a special base. Avoid `href="#"` as a fake action. The classroom sandbox blocks external network behavior deliberately; use local fragments here.

chapters.title: Lists, quotations, code and meaningful text
chapters.mental:
Lists express relationships that paragraphs do not. An ordered list describes a sequence where position matters. An unordered list groups peers without requiring order. A description list pairs terms with explanations. These structures help reading tools announce item counts and relationships. A row of hyphens in plain text may look like a list but does not expose that structure.

A quotation identifies borrowed language and should have a source when appropriate. Code identifies literal program text, while pre preserves whitespace. The combination pre and code is useful for multiline snippets. Long lines still need an overflow policy. Never use a quotation element simply to indent text or a list merely to create a visual column.
chapters.anatomy: A list contains li elements; nested lists belong inside the parent li they elaborate. A description list contains dt terms and dd explanations. A short inline token uses code without pre. Literal less-than signs in displayed code must be escaped because the containing HTML still has to parse correctly.
examples: The order is part of the instructions.
A numbered sequence exposes three ordered steps.
Escaping prevents the example from becoming live markup.
The displayed code contains literal paragraph tags.
tasks: Choose a list type for steps and an unordered tool collection.
Steps use ol; interchangeable peer tools use ul.
Add two vocabulary terms with definitions.
A dl contains paired dt and dd elements.
Build a study checklist with a code example and glossary.
The page exposes list, code and definition structures without relying on spacing.
Repair a nested list placed as a sibling of its parent item.
The nested list belongs inside the associated li.
Test a long code line in a narrow preview.
The code region can scroll without making the entire page horizontally overflow.
Explain the difference between preserving whitespace and preserving meaning.
Pre preserves formatting; semantic elements additionally communicate content roles.
chapters.mistakes: Do not use nonbreaking spaces to build layout columns. Avoid unescaped code snippets that accidentally create real tags. A screenshot can hide these structural errors, so inspect the tree.

chapters.title: Images, SVG, alternatives and media decisions
chapters.mental:
Alternative text communicates an image's purpose in its context. A decorative image may use empty alt text so it does not add noise. An informative image needs a concise equivalent; a complex chart usually needs surrounding explanation or a data table as well. A filename is rarely useful alternative text. The same picture can need different alternatives in different contexts because the task differs.

A figure groups self-contained media with a caption. A caption is visible to everyone, while an alternative serves when the image is unavailable or not visually perceived. SVG describes vector geometry and can be written inline, which keeps our fixtures offline. A viewBox defines internal coordinates; CSS controls the displayed dimensions. Width and height reserve space and reduce unexpected layout movement.
chapters.anatomy: For inline SVG, connect a title and description using `aria-labelledby`, and use `role="img"` for a meaningful standalone illustration. Decorative SVG can be hidden from assistive technology. Use a textual list when exact values matter. Audio and video require captions or transcripts, appropriate controls and deliberate autoplay decisions; no media downloads are required by this lesson.
examples: The alternative describes the information relevant to this page.
The dimensions reserve space; the alternative conveys a useful location.
The named title is inside the vector image.

<svg viewBox="0 0 100 30" role="img" aria-labelledby="label">
  <title id="label">Three completed lessons</title>
  <rect width="60" height="20" />
</svg>
A vector shape has a textual accessible name.
tasks: Choose alternatives for decorative and informative images.
Decorative images have empty alternatives; informative ones convey task-relevant meaning.
Add a visible caption without repeating a verbose alternative.
Caption and alternative serve complementary roles.
Create an offline SVG progress illustration with a textual equivalent.
The image has an accessible name and the numeric progress is visible as text.
Explain why chart alt text saying chart is insufficient.
It names the object but omits the information the reader needs.
Shrink the preview and preserve the SVG aspect ratio.
The illustration scales while labels and the textual equivalent remain readable.
Plan an accessible video lesson without autoplay.
Provide controls, captions and a transcript, with deliberate download size and motion choices.
chapters.mistakes: An image loading successfully says nothing about its alternative. Avoid remote placeholders in offline examples. Do not convert all useful text into an image just to control typography.

chapters.title: Data tables, captions and header relationships
chapters.mental:
A table represents data whose meaning depends on row and column relationships. It should not be the default layout tool for unrelated page regions. A caption identifies the table's topic, units or scope. Header cells identify a column or row so a reading tool can associate values with their context. Visual boldness alone cannot establish that relationship.

Keep a table simple when possible. A dataset with two independent header axes can use column and row scope. More complex spans may require explicit header associations and careful testing. For a narrow screen, preserve the relationships instead of hiding important columns. A scrollable region can keep the table intact when the data genuinely needs two dimensions.
chapters.anatomy: Use thead for the header group, tbody for records, th for headers and td for values. `scope="col"` identifies a column header and `scope="row"` identifies a row header. Numeric alignment is presentation, while the units belong in the content. Tables must remain useful when colors or zebra stripes are unavailable.
examples: The header explicitly identifies what the numeric cells measure.
The second column has a named unit.
The subject identifies the row across its values.
40 is associated with HTML and the Minutes column.
tasks: Explain what a single cell value means with both headers.
40 means forty minutes of HTML study, not an unlabeled count.
Add a caption that states the reporting period.
The visible caption explains the table's scope.
Build a three-row study table with correct header relationships.
The caption, row headers and column headers identify every value.
Replace a table used to align unrelated navigation and article content.
Use semantic regions plus CSS layout rather than false data relationships.
Inspect the table at a narrow width without deleting data.
A bounded overflow region keeps all columns reachable.
Explain when a chart should keep a supporting table.
Exact values and nonvisual interpretation often benefit from a tabular equivalent.
chapters.mistakes: Do not confuse a table caption with an unrelated heading several paragraphs away. Avoid empty header cells when a meaningful label exists. A DOM assertion cannot prove a screen reader's announcement behavior.

chapters.title: Forms: labels, controls and successful values
chapters.mental:
A form collects values for an action. A label names a control; a placeholder offers a short example and disappears during entry, so it cannot replace a label. A control's id connects it to a label. Its name identifies the value when a browser constructs form data. These are different responsibilities, and a visible input without a name may not be submitted.

Choose the native control that matches the task. A select presents a bounded choice, a textarea accepts multiline text, and checkboxes represent independent choices. A radio group represents one choice among alternatives and shares a name. A fieldset and legend describe a related group. Native controls provide interaction and accessibility behavior that a custom drawing would need to recreate.
chapters.anatomy: Connect `label for="topic"` with `input id="topic" name="topic"`. A button inside a form defaults to submission, so specify its type. Disabled controls are not included in submitted form data; readonly text controls can still contribute values. This offline preview prevents real submission. Inspect control values and labels without contacting a backend.
examples: Identifier and submitted name have separate jobs.
Selecting the label focuses its associated input.
A legend provides a group-level question.
The checkbox has a label and a group context.
tasks: Predict the different roles of id and name.
Id supports document relationships; name identifies the submitted field.
Add a textarea with a persistent label.
The label remains available while the user types.
Build a study-preferences form with three native control types.
Every control has a useful label, stable name and suitable type.
Diagnose a field missing from submitted values.
Check name, disabled state and the control's successful-value rules.
Navigate the form using only Tab and Space.
Each enabled control is reachable and can be operated without a pointer.
Explain why form appearance cannot establish server validation.
Client controls guide entry; a server must independently validate incoming data.
chapters.mistakes: Do not use only placeholder text or a nearby unconnected paragraph as a label. Avoid nested forms. A control's visible value can differ from the value a server ultimately trusts.

chapters.title: Form constraints, errors and helpful recovery
chapters.mental:
Validation checks whether input satisfies a contract. Browser constraint validation gives immediate feedback through attributes such as required, type, min and maxlength. It improves the interaction but is not a security boundary because a client can bypass it or send a request without using the form at all. A server must repeat the relevant validation and authorization decisions.

An error message should identify the field, explain the problem and offer a useful correction without losing the user's work. Color alone is insufficient. Connect instructions and errors with aria-describedby, and use aria-invalid when an actual invalid state has been identified. Do not mark every untouched field invalid when the page first opens.
chapters.anatomy: `checkValidity()` reports whether a control meets its constraints. `reportValidity()` also requests the browser's feedback interface. An empty required field is invalid, while a non-required empty email field may be valid. Email type checks syntax, not whether the mailbox exists or belongs to the user. This lesson uses native constraints and explicit explanatory text; it does not send data.
examples: The contract is visible in the label and attributes.

<label for="minutes">Minutes, 5 to 120</label
><input id="minutes" name="minutes" type="number" min="5" max="120" required />
An empty value fails required; 4 fails the minimum.
Help remains available while entering data.
Use at least three characters.
The input references its visible instruction.
tasks: Predict required, minimum and maximum outcomes for empty, 4, 30 and 121.
Empty, 4 and 121 fail; 30 satisfies the numeric bounds.
Add a clear unit and range to a control's label.
The rule is understandable before an error occurs.
Build a bounded study-time form with linked help.
The user can identify the rule, enter a valid value and retain it after a failed attempt.
Explain why type=email does not prove mailbox ownership.
It checks a syntactic format, not identity or delivery.
Test validation with keyboard and an empty field.
The error is discoverable and the entered values are preserved.
Separate client feedback from server-side acceptance.
The backend repeats contract checks and authorization regardless of browser validation.
chapters.mistakes: Do not erase all fields after one invalid input. Do not imply red borders alone are adequate. Programmatic assignment and real user editing can differ for some constraints, so test actual interaction as well as scripted values.

chapters.title: CSS rules, selectors and the cascade
chapters.mental:
A CSS rule has a selector and a declaration block. The selector chooses elements; each declaration sets a property to a value. Several rules can match the same element. The cascade resolves conflicts using origin, importance, layer order, specificity, scoping proximity where applicable and source order. Specificity is not the entire algorithm. A later rule wins only after the earlier priorities tie.

Inheritance is another mechanism: some properties, such as text color, naturally pass from a parent to children unless overridden. Other properties, such as margins, normally do not. A value inherited from a parent does not beat a declaration directly targeting the child just because the parent selector is more specific. Browser developer tools reveal which rule won and which declaration was crossed out.
chapters.anatomy: Start with low-specificity class selectors for reusable components. `.note` targets a class, `#summary` targets one id, and `p` targets an element type. `color: #17324d` is a declaration. Use the computed-style view to inspect the resolved value. Avoid adding important flags repeatedly to fight a conflict whose origin you have not identified.
examples: A class describes a group of elements.
Every element with class note receives those declarations.
Source order decides after the relevant priorities tie.
Dark red wins for matching elements in this simple unlayered example.
tasks: Predict the winning color in the second example.
The later equally specific declaration wins.
Move a shared text color to a parent and inspect inheritance.
Children inherit it unless a direct declaration overrides it.
Style two note cards using one low-specificity class.
Both cards share styling without duplicate ids or inline declarations.
Diagnose a crossed-out declaration in developer tools.
Identify the winning rule and the cascade reason rather than guessing.
Add a child color rule under a highly specific parent selector.
A direct declaration on the child overrides an otherwise inherited color.
Explain why specificity alone does not describe the cascade.
Origin, importance and layer ordering can be decided before selector specificity.
chapters.mistakes: Avoid solving an unknown conflict by escalating selectors. Inline style, important declarations and cascade layers have separate priorities. Devtools evidence is more informative than visually similar colors.

chapters.title: The box model, sizing and overflow
chapters.mental:
Every rendered box has content, optional padding, a border and an outside margin. With the default content-box sizing, a declared width describes the content, so padding and borders add to the outer width. With border-box sizing, the declared width includes the content, padding and borders. Margins remain outside either calculation. This distinction explains many layouts that unexpectedly exceed a parent.

Overflow occurs when content needs more room than the available box. Hiding overflow can conceal essential information; scrolling or wrapping may preserve it. Long unbroken strings and images are frequent sources of overflow. A fixed height can clip translated text, enlarged fonts or error messages, so prefer content-driven height unless the interaction truly requires a bounded region.
chapters.anatomy: For a 200px content-box with 20px left and right padding and 2px borders, outer width is 244px. For a 200px border-box, the content width becomes 156px. Set a consistent box-sizing rule on all elements and pseudo-elements. Use max-inline-size to constrain readable width without assuming the writing direction.
examples: The declared content width excludes padding and border.
The declared width now contains the interior spacing.
tasks: Calculate outer widths for the two examples.
They are 244px and 200px, before margins.
Add border-box sizing to a document and inspect one card.
The declared width matches the border-box width.
Build a readable card that contains a long identifier.
The identifier wraps or scrolls locally without overflowing the page.
Repair a fixed height that clips a validation message.
Use content-driven height or an explicitly accessible bounded scroll region.
Increase text size and inspect overflow.
Essential text remains visible and controls remain reachable.
Explain which dimensions margin does and does not affect.
Margins add external separation but are not included in either box-sizing width.
chapters.mistakes: Do not use overflow:hidden to hide a layout bug without checking lost content. Vertical margins can collapse in ordinary block layout, while flex and grid layout have different rules. Inspect box measurements directly.

chapters.title: Typography, units and readable content
chapters.mental:
Typography controls the effort required to read. A font stack lists preferred fonts followed by a generic fallback, so text remains usable when a particular font is absent. This course uses system fonts and makes no external font request. Relative units allow the design to respond to user settings. A rem is relative to the root font size; em often depends on the current element's font size, with property-specific details.

Line length, line height and spacing interact. Very long lines make it difficult to find the next line; very short lines create constant interruptions. A max-width expressed in ch can approximate a readable character measure, though it is based on the zero glyph width rather than an exact count of all characters. A unitless line-height scales naturally with the element's font size.
chapters.anatomy: Use `font: 1rem/1.6 system-ui, sans-serif` to set size, unitless line-height and family. Avoid fixing the root to a tiny pixel size to make arithmetic convenient. Preserve user zoom. Headings can use a bounded fluid size with clamp, while body text should remain comfortable and predictable. Text alignment is content-sensitive; full justification can create distracting gaps in narrow columns.
examples: The column stays bounded even on a large monitor.
Paragraphs have a bounded measure and relative text size.
Clamp supplies a minimum, preferred fluid size and maximum.
The heading grows with width within the given bounds.
tasks: Explain the reference for rem and a typical em use.
Rem uses the root font size; em commonly scales with the relevant element's font size.
Apply a system font stack without network dependencies.
The page remains readable offline on different operating systems.
Build a reading page with bounded measure and scalable headings.
Text stays comfortable at wide and narrow sizes without fixed-height clipping.
Diagnose text that overlaps after zooming.
Inspect fixed heights, line heights and positioned containers rather than disabling zoom.
Test at increased browser zoom with long content.
Reading order, text visibility and controls remain intact.
Explain why ch is a useful approximation rather than a word-count guarantee.
It measures the font's zero glyph, and actual character widths vary.
chapters.mistakes: Do not disable pinch zoom or set user-scalable=no. A brand font is optional; readable content is not. Test actual enlargement because a screenshot at one size cannot expose clipping.

chapters.title: Color, contrast, focus and accessible states
chapters.mental:
Color can group information, but it cannot be the only carrier of an essential distinction. A failed status should have words or an icon with an accessible name as well as a color. Contrast is the difference in luminance that makes foreground content distinguishable from its background. A pleasing palette does not automatically provide readable text or usable controls. Test the actual foreground-background pair in each state, including hover, focus, disabled and error.

Focus identifies the element receiving keyboard input. Removing the browser's outline without a replacement makes navigation difficult or impossible for many users. The focus-visible pseudo-class lets the browser apply its heuristics for when focus needs a visible indicator. A control can also require an adequately sized target and enough spacing from neighboring controls.
chapters.anatomy: Define a small set of tokens for text, background, accent and borders, then inspect their combinations. Use an outline with an offset so it is not hidden by the border. A status element can contain the word Ready or Needs attention; color reinforces that label. Prefer explicit text to a legend that a reader must memorize.
examples: A clear outline remains distinct from the control border.
Keyboard focus has a visible indicator.
Words preserve the information without color.
The status is understandable in monochrome.
tasks: Identify the missing information in a red-only error dot.
The user needs a textual error meaning and a useful recovery action.
Add a focus-visible style without removing focus support.
Keyboard focus is visibly distinguishable from hover.
Build status cards whose meaning does not depend on color.
Each card contains a clear label, readable text and visible interactive focus.
Diagnose a focus ring clipped by overflow.
Inspect the ancestor clipping boundary and provide space or a different visible indicator.
Inspect the page in a forced-colors or high-contrast setting.
Native boundaries and meaningful labels remain available; document actual browser behavior.
Explain why one palette check does not qualify every interaction state.
Backgrounds and foregrounds can change per state, so each important combination needs review.
chapters.mistakes: Do not calculate contrast against an assumed background when an overlay or image changes it. A custom focus ring that resembles hover may still confuse users. Automated checks complement real keyboard review.

chapters.title: Normal flow, display and positioning
chapters.mental:
Normal flow is the browser's default arrangement of content. Block boxes generally stack in the block direction and inline content flows within lines. Understanding this default prevents unnecessary positioning. Display changes how an element participates in layout; it does not change its underlying HTML meaning. A paragraph made display:flex remains a paragraph semantically.

Positioning modifies placement relative to a containing block or scroll container. Relative positioning keeps the element's original space while offsetting its painted position. Absolute positioning removes it from ordinary flow and uses a containing block, often the nearest positioned ancestor. Fixed positioning is often tied to the viewport but transformed ancestors can affect that behavior. Sticky positioning depends on a scroll container and an inset threshold.
chapters.anatomy: Use position:relative on a card only when it intentionally establishes the containing block for an absolute badge. Keep the main article content in flow. A sticky section label needs an inset such as top:0 and sufficient scroll space. Avoid putting every element at exact pixel coordinates; content length and viewport width will change.
examples: The second paragraph follows the first in normal flow.
Only the badge is taken out of flow.
The badge is positioned relative to the card.
tasks: Predict whether relative positioning frees the original space.
It does not; the original layout space remains.
Turn a group of inline links into a block navigation list.
Display changes the arrangement without changing navigation semantics.
Build a card with an intentional positioned badge and flowing content.
Long body text expands the card while the badge stays in its reserved corner.
Diagnose an absolute label overlapping enlarged text.
Provide sufficient reserved space or return the label to normal flow.
Add a long paragraph and narrow the preview.
Content remains readable and the badge does not obscure it.
Explain the containing block used by an absolute element.
Identify the actual ancestor that establishes it, rather than assuming it is always the viewport.
chapters.mistakes: Sticky positioning can fail because an ancestor creates an unexpected scroll container. Z-index does not repair an incorrect containing block. Keep the reading order in the source meaningful.

chapters.title: Flexbox: one-dimensional layout and resilient navigation
chapters.mental:
Flexbox distributes space among items primarily along one axis. The main axis follows flex-direction, while the cross axis is perpendicular. justify-content distributes available space along the main axis; align-items aligns items along the cross axis. The names do not permanently mean horizontal and vertical because direction can change.

Flexible items have a basis and rules for growing or shrinking. A row of long labels may overflow if wrapping is disabled or if an item's automatic minimum size prevents shrinking. `min-inline-size:0` is often useful for a flex child that must allow its text to wrap or truncate deliberately. Flexbox is a layout tool, not permission to reorder content into a confusing keyboard sequence.
chapters.anatomy: Use display:flex, gap and flex-wrap:wrap for a simple responsive group. `flex: 1 1 12rem` gives an initial basis and permits growth and shrinkage. Set `align-items:stretch` when equal cross-axis size supports the component. Keep DOM order aligned with intended reading and focus order rather than using order to create a contradictory visual sequence.
examples: Wrapping preserves reachable links when space is limited.
Items form additional rows rather than overflowing.
The basis expresses a preference rather than an inflexible width.
Cards share available space and can wrap.
tasks: Name the axes for flex-direction:column.
The main axis is vertical in the usual horizontal writing mode; the cross axis is horizontal.
Add gap between navigation items without per-item margins.
Spacing is owned by the container and stays consistent when wrapping.
Build a wrapping navigation bar and flexible card row.
Long labels stay reachable at narrow widths and DOM order remains logical.
Diagnose a flex child that refuses to shrink.
Inspect its minimum size, long content and flex-basis before forcing overflow hidden.
Test one item, many items and a very long label.
The layout remains readable without relying on exactly three equal strings.
Explain when Flexbox fits better than Grid.
Use Flexbox for distributing items along one primary dimension; use Grid for explicit two-dimensional alignment.
chapters.mistakes: Do not equate justify-content with horizontal alignment universally. Visual order changes do not necessarily change keyboard order. A perfectly aligned screenshot is insufficient if navigation becomes confusing.

chapters.title: Grid: tracks, gaps and two-dimensional alignment
chapters.mental:
Grid arranges items along rows and columns. A track is the space between two adjacent grid lines. Fractional fr units share remaining space after fixed sizes and gaps have been considered. They are not a fixed percentage of the full container. An item's minimum content contribution can still affect track size, which explains why a long unbroken value may widen an apparently equal grid.

Grid is useful when rows and columns must align across a collection. An auto-fit repeat with minmax can create as many columns as fit a preferred minimum, then distribute remaining room. The minimum must still fit a narrow viewport. A layout should adapt to its content, not depend on one device model or a fixed card count.
chapters.anatomy: Use `grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(min(100%,14rem),1fr))` for a resilient card collection. The inner min permits a track to fit a container narrower than the preferred minimum. `gap` adds separation without changing source order. Named grid areas are useful for a page shell, but the source order must remain understandable when the layout collapses.

chapters.title: Responsive layouts and content-driven breakpoints
chapters.mental:
Responsive design lets one document work across available sizes and user settings. A breakpoint is a condition where a layout needs to change, not a permanent name for a device. A phone can have a wide landscape viewport; a desktop window can be narrow. Start with content that works in a small space and add more complex arrangements only when enough room exists.

The viewport metadata tells mobile browsers to use the device's layout width rather than a historical wide page assumption. Flexible widths, wrapping and content-driven heights solve many problems before a media query is necessary. A responsive page must also survive enlarged text, translations and long values, not merely a list of screen widths.
chapters.anatomy: Use a base single-column layout and a min-width media query for a wider arrangement. Relative units in queries support a design tied to text scale. Inspect where the content becomes cramped and choose the breakpoint from that evidence. Keep the navigation visible or provide a fully accessible disclosure rather than simply hiding it on small screens.
examples: The ordinary layout works without a query.

chapters.mistakes: Do not hide essential actions just because space is limited. Avoid fixed viewport-height panels that trap content behind mobile browser chrome. Test actual text growth and settled layout.

chapters.title: Custom properties, tokens and component themes
chapters.mental:
A design token names a recurring design decision such as a spacing step, text color or border radius. CSS custom properties store values that participate in the cascade and can be scoped to a component. A variable name should communicate its purpose, such as --surface or --space-small, rather than merely its current value. That allows the value to change while the role remains stable.

Custom properties are resolved where they are used and usually inherit. A card can override a small set of tokens while retaining the same component rules. A fallback in var supplies a value when a variable is missing or invalid in the relevant way, but a custom property can still produce an invalid declaration at computed-value time. Test the final computed result instead of assuming any string is suitable for any property.
chapters.anatomy: Define shared defaults at :root and override them on a component class. `background:var(--surface,white)` uses the current scope's value. Keep semantic text labels independent of theme color. A theme change must preserve contrast and focus behavior, not merely update an accent swatch.

chapters.title: Pseudo-classes, pseudo-elements and stateful styling
chapters.mental:
A pseudo-class selects an element based on a condition such as focus, checked state or its position among siblings. A pseudo-element represents a stylable part associated with an element, such as before or after. Generated decorative content can enrich presentation, but essential instructions should exist as real document content because generated content has inconsistent accessibility implications.

State should remain grounded in a real control or application contract. Styling a checkbox's checked state makes use of built-in behavior. A decorative class named active does not prove that a control is selected, and CSS cannot perform server authorization. Use native state first and add custom state only with a clear interaction model.
chapters.anatomy: `:focus-within` matches a container while one of its descendants has focus. `input:checked + span` selects a neighboring label fragment after a checked input. Attribute selectors can target a declared state, but the application is responsible for keeping that state accurate. Hover must be an enhancement because touch and keyboard interactions may not provide the same hover behavior.
examples: The container helps the user locate the current task.

A pseudo-class selects an existing state; a pseudo-element styles a represented part.

chapters.mistakes: A hover-only menu can exclude keyboard users. Generated text can be skipped or announced unexpectedly. Keep meaningful text in the document and let CSS reinforce it.

chapters.title: Transitions, motion and reduced-motion preferences
chapters.mental:
Motion can explain a change, but it can also distract, delay a task or cause discomfort. A transition interpolates between property values when state changes. An animation uses named keyframes over time. Neither should be required to understand essential content. Begin with the static usable state and add restrained motion only when it improves orientation.

Animating layout-affecting properties can trigger repeated layout work, while transform and opacity often allow more efficient compositing. This is not a guarantee of smooth performance because element size, painting and the device still matter. Measure actual behavior rather than assuming that a property name proves efficiency. Continuous decorative motion rarely helps a reading task.
chapters.anatomy: Specify the properties to transition instead of transition:all, which can animate unrelated future changes. The prefers-reduced-motion media query lets a page respond to a user's preference. A reduced-motion rule can remove movement while retaining a color or outline change. Do not use a tiny but nonzero duration as a universal accessibility strategy; understand the interaction's required events and states.

A transition follows a property change; an animation follows a named timeline.

chapters.mistakes: Do not make reduced motion disable the action itself. Avoid infinite animations in reading material. Test the preference in a real browser because source presence does not prove the rule won the cascade.

chapters.title: Container queries and reusable responsive components
chapters.mental:
A media query responds to the viewport or device environment. A container query can respond to an ancestor container's size, which is useful when the same component appears in a wide article and a narrow sidebar on the same page. The component should adapt to the space it receives instead of assuming it always spans the viewport.

Size containment changes how a container participates in sizing. Declare it deliberately on an appropriate wrapper, not on every element. A size query targets an eligible ancestor, not the queried element itself. Keep a useful base layout so the component remains readable in environments where the query is unsupported or never matches.
chapters.anatomy: Set `container-type:inline-size` on a wrapper, optionally with a container-name. Inside `@container`, adjust the descendant component when its wrapper is wide enough. Prefer logical dimensions so the design does not unnecessarily assume a writing direction. This chapter demonstrates progressive enhancement; the unqueried stacked card remains functional.

chapters.title: CSS architecture, layers and maintainable components
chapters.mental:
A stylesheet is easier to change when responsibilities are visible. Base rules describe document defaults, component rules describe reusable structures, and narrowly named utilities make deliberate local adjustments. These categories are a design choice, not a browser feature by themselves. Cascade layers let authors establish an explicit ordering among groups of declarations without continually increasing selector specificity.

For normal author declarations, later layers take priority over earlier layers, and unlayered normal declarations have priority over layered normal declarations. Important declarations reverse layer priority, which is one reason indiscriminate important usage makes reasoning harder. A good architecture keeps selectors understandable and limits the area a change can affect.
chapters.anatomy: Declare the layer order once with `@layer base, components, utilities`. Put actual rules inside those layers. Keep component names tied to a useful responsibility such as lesson-card, not a visual accident such as left-blue-box. Test a component in more than one surrounding context to expose accidental ancestor dependencies.

chapters.mistakes: A named architecture cannot prevent global selectors from leaking. Do not put every exception in an unlayered file because that silently bypasses the policy. Keep examples small enough to trace.

chapters.title: Print styles, progressive enhancement and resilient delivery
chapters.mental:
Progressive enhancement starts from useful content and adds capabilities when the environment supports them. A document should communicate its core information before advanced styling or scripts run. This does not mean every application must offer identical features in every environment; it means essential requirements and fallbacks are deliberate rather than accidental.

Print is a different presentation context. Navigation controls that are useful on screen can waste space on paper, while a visible URL or document title may become more valuable. A print stylesheet can remove decoration, preserve contrast and avoid splitting small related blocks. It cannot guarantee the printer, paper size or user settings, so inspect the browser's print preview before making claims.
chapters.anatomy: Use `@media print` for print-specific rules and `@supports` for a feature-dependent enhancement. Keep the base rule valid independently. Avoid hiding the actual article while removing navigation. `break-inside:avoid` is a request to the fragmentation system, not a promise that an arbitrarily large element fits on one page.

chapters.mistakes: Do not confuse feature detection with browser sniffing. Avoid claiming print quality from a screen screenshot. A large table may need its own print strategy rather than an indiscriminate no-break rule.

chapters.title: HTML and CSS milestone: an accessible learning portal
chapters.mental:
A portal combines structure, navigation and repeated components around a user goal. Begin with the tasks: finding a topic, understanding prerequisites, choosing an action and reading progress. The information architecture groups content so those tasks are discoverable. A beautiful collection of cards is not enough if every label is vague or the reading order hides the main choice.

This milestone integrates the earlier mechanisms without requiring a framework. Semantic headings establish the outline, native links provide navigation, Grid or Flexbox distributes cards, and tokens maintain consistent spacing and color. Progress labels remain textual. The project uses synthetic data and does not claim persistent accounts or a working backend.

Implement the smallest coherent page, then audit the settled state at multiple widths. Keep appearance checks separate from structural checks because each can pass while the other fails.

chapters.title: Connect HTML to JavaScript: DOM, events and safe text
chapters.mental:
The document object model is the browser's live tree of elements. JavaScript can select a node, observe an event and update content. HTML supplies the structure, CSS supplies presentation, and JavaScript handles behavior. Start with a native button so keyboard activation and focus work without reimplementation. The event listener is a function called when a matching event occurs; it is not the same as calling the function immediately while registering it.

Keep state separate from the text that displays it. A numeric count in a variable is the source of truth; a render function translates it into a label. Reading the current label and repeatedly parsing it back into a number couples business state to presentation. Use textContent for plain user text because it creates text rather than parsing markup.
chapters.anatomy:
`document.querySelector('#add')` returns a matching element or null. `addEventListener('click', handler)` registers a function. Update the number, then render the new value to an output element. Query elements after they exist, for example with a script at the end of the body. For JavaScript syntax, revisit the JavaScript foundations and browser chapters rather than treating this lesson as a substitute for that route.

A classic inline script runs when the parser reaches it. A script in the head cannot assume that later body elements already exist. Separate classic script tags share the document's global lexical environment, while a module has its own scope and strict semantics. DOMContentLoaded fires after parsing and the relevant deferred script work; it does not mean every image has loaded. The load event describes the later document load boundary. Register a listener before its event occurs, or inspect readyState when code can be loaded at different times.

An external classic script with defer preserves document order and waits for parsing. Async scripts do not provide that same ordering guarantee. Defer does not turn an inline classic script into a deferred one. Inline modules use real module semantics, including top-level this being undefined. The classroom supports inline modules but blocks external script files and imports. Study multi-file loading in a separately prepared local project rather than weakening the preview policy.

The state is numeric and independent of its label.

chapters.title: Disclosures, dialogs and focus management
chapters.mental:
A disclosure reveals content in the current document, while a dialog creates a focused interaction context. These are different patterns and should not be chosen only for visual style. Native details and summary elements provide a useful disclosure without JavaScript. A modal dialog changes which content can be interacted with and needs a clear way to close, an accessible name and sensible focus restoration.

Focus is part of the interaction's state. When a dialog opens, the user should land in a meaningful place. When it closes, focus usually returns to the control that opened it if that control still exists. Keyboard users must not become trapped in an accidental custom implementation. Native dialog behavior supplies important mechanics, but authors still own labeling, content order and testing.
chapters.anatomy: Use details with summary for optional explanation. Use a dialog element and showModal when a true modal task is justified. A form with method=dialog can close the dialog; this local behavior is distinct from a network form submission. The offline preview may restrict submission APIs, so this reference closes explicitly through the dialog API and keeps all state local.

chapters.title: Accessible form feedback with a pure validation function
chapters.mental:
Validation becomes easier to test when a pure function receives data and returns errors without touching the document. The browser layer then displays those errors and moves focus only when it helps recovery. This separation lets the same input contract be tested with normal, missing and boundary values before considering visual presentation. It does not remove the need for backend validation.

An error summary gives a user an overview after an attempted action. Field-level messages explain how to repair specific values. Connect those messages to controls and preserve entered values. Avoid announcing a long stream of errors on every keystroke. The timing of feedback is a product decision that should reduce confusion rather than punish incomplete typing.
chapters.anatomy: The reference uses a button to validate local values without submitting a form. Convert the input string carefully, reject empty strings before Number conversion and check Number.isFinite. Return an error list, then render it with textContent. Set aria-invalid only after a failed check. A valid result is a local observation, not a stored request.

chapters.title: Data interfaces: filtering tables and honest visual summaries
chapters.mental:
A data interface connects records to a representation. Keep the original records separate from the filtered view so a user can clear a filter without reconstructing lost input. A table is useful for exact values; a chart emphasizes patterns. Both need labels, units and a declared handling of missing values. A visually impressive chart can still tell an incorrect story if its filtering or scale is wrong.

This lesson uses a tiny local array and a semantic table. A select changes the derived records, then one render function replaces the table body with safely created cells. An empty result receives an explicit message rather than an unexplained blank area. The JavaScript D3 specialization builds on the same principles for richer scales, joins and interaction; it is a continuation, not a replacement for data validation.
chapters.anatomy: Use array.filter to derive records without mutating the source array. Create cells with createElement and textContent. Count the resulting rows and compare with the stated filter. For later D3 work, preserve stable record identities and separate data transformation from visual encoding. Never imply that a client-side filter is access control over confidential data already sent to the browser.

chapters.title: Browser trust boundaries: text, origins and policy
chapters.mental:
An origin is generally a combination of scheme, host and port. The browser uses origins to separate access to data and documents. The same-origin policy is not a complete application security system; a server still needs authentication, authorization and deliberate cross-origin behavior. CORS is a protocol for relaxing some browser response-reading restrictions, not a mechanism that makes an unsafe endpoint safe.

Injection occurs when data is interpreted as code or structure in a context where it should remain data. textContent avoids HTML parsing for text, while building an href still requires a separate URL policy. Content Security Policy can reduce what a document may load or execute, but it is a defense layer rather than a replacement for correct output handling. The classroom preview is deliberately isolated and network restricted.
chapters.anatomy: Treat rendering contexts separately: HTML text, quoted HTML attribute, URL, JavaScript and CSS each have different rules. This reference renders an attack-shaped string only as text. No attack is performed against another site. A sandboxed iframe can have an opaque origin, so do not assume localStorage, cookies or a same-origin parent API exists inside the preview.

chapters.title: Browser quality: tests, performance and independent review
chapters.mental:
Quality is a set of observable contracts. A structural test can check that a button has a label. An interaction test can check that it changes the intended value. A visual inspection can reveal clipping after resizing. An assistive-technology review can expose an announcement problem. No single kind of test proves all of these. Plan the evidence around the behavior you claim.

Performance also requires a defined workload and measurement boundary. Loading, parsing, scripting, layout, painting and network transfer contribute differently. A tiny function timer is not page-load performance. Warm caches, device speed, background activity and instrumentation affect measurements. Report the conditions and distributions instead of declaring an arbitrary universal millisecond target.
chapters.anatomy: Use explicit assertions that throw on failure rather than relying only on console.assert. Keep a deterministic fixture for logic tests and a separate manual checklist for keyboard, zoom, narrow width, print and reduced motion. Measure a bounded task with performance.now only when explaining that local task. Do not interpret a microbenchmark as a production capacity claim.

Explain what evidence would justify a production readiness claim.

chapters.mistakes: Avoid tests that merely search for a success string without exercising behavior. Do not erase a failure transcript when retrying. A successful browser run applies to that tested browser and source, not automatically to all devices.

chapters.title: PHP begins: interpreter, CLI and server execution
chapters.mental:
PHP is a programming language whose interpreter executes source instructions. In the classroom, a Linux CLI worker runs one file and captures its output. On a web server, a PHP runtime can instead receive request context and produce an HTTP response. These environments share language syntax but expose different inputs and lifecycle behavior. Printing a string that looks like HTML does not turn a CLI process into a web server.

PHP source begins with an opening tag, and statements commonly end with semicolons. Variables begin with a dollar sign. A comment explains source without executing it. Echo writes output; it does not return a value from a function or save data to a database. We start with literal strings and a tiny computed value so each step is visible.
chapters.anatomy: Use a pure PHP file beginning with `<?php`, followed by `declare(strict_types=1);` before other statements. Strict typing affects certain scalar type coercions at function call boundaries; it does not turn PHP into a statically typed language. Omit the closing tag in a pure PHP file to avoid accidental trailing output. Syntax errors occur before the intended program can run, while runtime errors occur during execution.
examples: A string literal becomes text in stdout.
One greeting line appears in the CLI output.
A variable makes the data's role explicit.
The dot operator concatenates the label and value.
tasks: Predict which characters in the greeting source appear in output.
The opening tag and echo keyword do not appear; the string content does.
Change the planned minutes while preserving the label.
Only the numeric portion changes.
Write a PHP program that prints a study topic and computed duration.
The program runs in the CLI worker and produces two clearly labeled values.
Diagnose a missing semicolon as a parse error.
